title: Controlling mosquitoes with semiochemicals: a review

subsections.subsection_title: Malaria Vector Control Context and Emerging Challenges
subsections.content:
Malaria vector control over the past two decades has been driven primarily by long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS), which together account for much of the decline in Plasmodium falciparum burden in Africa. Yet these gains have plateaued in many settings, highlighting the operational and biological limits of interventions that act mainly against mosquitoes feeding or resting indoors [3].

A central challenge is residual malaria transmission, defined as transmission that persists even after high coverage with effective LLINs and/or IRS. This residual component is sustained by vectors that avoid treated surfaces, bite outdoors or at times when people are not protected, feed on animals, or rest outside houses; importantly, such transmission can remain substantial even where vectors are physiologically susceptible to insecticides [1]. Parallel to these behavioral limitations, intensifying insecticide resistance further threatens the durability of current control programs and strengthens the case for new delivery systems and complementary interventions [3].

Emerging ecological change also reshapes malaria risk. The invasion of Anopheles stephensi into Djibouti and Ethiopia raises the prospect of large-scale urban malaria in Africa because this species is well adapted to man-made water storage habitats and densely populated cities, in contrast to the historically more rural bias of African malaria transmission [2]. In this context, house-based innovations such as eave tubes illustrate the broader shift toward tools that exploit mosquito behavior while reducing human exposure to insecticides and complementing, rather than replacing, LLINs and IRS [3]. These pressures together provide the immediate public health rationale for renewed interest in semiochemical and other behaviorally informed control strategies.

subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Mosquito Olfaction and Host-Seeking
subsections.content:
Mosquito host seeking is a staged sensory process in which olfaction provides the dominant long-range information used to detect and orient toward vertebrate hosts, whereas heat, moisture, and visual contrast contribute more strongly at closer range ref [4], ref [5]. The primary olfactory organs are the antennae and maxillary palps, which carry receptor neurons tuned to key host volatiles, most notably carbon dioxide on the palps and a broader repertoire of skin- and breath-derived compounds on the antennae ref [4], ref [5]. This sensory architecture underpins the characteristic activation, upwind flight, landing, and biting sequence of anautogenous female mosquitoes.

Foundational behavioral work showed that carbon dioxide is a general activator and orientation cue, but host discrimination depends on additional odor blends from skin emanations, breath, and other body-derived volatiles ref [4], ref [5]. In anthropophilic malaria vectors such as Anopheles gambiae, attraction to whole human odor, foot odor, sweat, and chemically similar microbial products indicated that host seeking is mediated by complex kairomonal mixtures rather than single universal attractants ref [4]. This complexity also helps explain why host preference varies markedly across mosquito taxa, from highly specialized human-feeding species to broadly opportunistic feeders ref [6].

Host-seeking behavior is further shaped by physiological state and ecological context. Nutritional reserves, age, gonotrophic stage, and prior sugar or blood feeding alter response thresholds to host cues, while species-specific host preference reflects both inherited sensory biases and plasticity driven by host availability ref [4], ref [6]. These foundations in mosquito olfaction are central to semiochemical control: identifying which odor blends activate, attract, or bias host choice is a prerequisite for designing lures, traps, and push-pull interventions that target malaria vectors with high behavioral specificity ref [4], ref [5].

Chemical-ecology research has translated increasingly well into operational attractant design by treating mosquito host seeking as a combinatorial problem rather than a search for a single “magic” cue. Iterative blend development showed that human-associated volatiles such as ammonia, lactic acid, and selected carboxylic acids can act synergistically, and that optimized synthetic lures may approach or exceed the attractiveness of human odor under field conditions ref [7], ref [3], ref [4], ref [5]. This progression established semiochemical blends as credible tools for surveillance, trapping, and behavioral manipulation of malaria vectors.

A key advance was the recognition that carbon dioxide is not merely a generic activator but a context-dependent organizer of odor blend efficacy. In Anopheles coluzzii, adding CO2 to a human-derived base blend significantly increased attraction and enabled certain C4 compounds, notably butan-1-amine and 3-methyl-1-butanol, to enhance rather than suppress behavioral responses, yielding an optimized five-component lure ref [7]. Related field studies likewise found that CO2 augments captures for synthetic host-odor blends, although its practical deployment remains constrained by logistics and cost in remote endemic settings ref [8], ref [4].

Attractant development has also broadened beyond vertebrate-host cues to include plant-derived semiochemicals relevant to sugar feeding. Field evaluation of linalool oxide-centered blends demonstrated that plant-based odors can attract Anopheles gambiae s.l. and An. funestus s.l., sometimes comparably to animal/human-derived lures, while also sampling males and engorged females that are less well represented in strictly host-based trapping paradigms ref [8]. This expansion is conceptually important because it links odor-bait technology to attractive toxic sugar bait strategies and to outdoor vector management, where residual transmission increasingly undermines indoor-focused control ref [8], ref [6].

Beyond host odours and trap chemistry, mosquito semiochemical research sits within a broader sensory-ecology framework in which olfaction is one component of integrated orientation. Comparative work on insect chemosensation shows that olfactory systems evolve under strong ecological selection, with receptor repertoires and peripheral sensilla shaped by habitat, resource use, and communication demands ref [9]. More generally, chemical signalling often emerges from pre-existing environmental cues, and many behaviourally active compounds first function as incidental information before being elaborated into true signals through selection on detectability and receiver response ref [11]. This perspective is useful for mosquitoes, where kairomones, pheromones, and plant- or host-derived volatiles likely occupy a continuum between cue exploitation and specialized communication.

Methodologically, progress in mosquito chemical ecology has depended increasingly on high-resolution behavioural phenotyping. Automated video tracking, including 2D and 3D flight reconstruction, has made it possible to quantify activation, plume following, landing, house-entry behaviour, and responses to multimodal cue combinations with far greater precision than trap catches alone ref [10]. These tools have clarified, for example, how CO2, heat, vision, and odor blends are integrated across different spatial scales and behavioural phases, and they provide a bridge between laboratory olfactometer assays and operational vector-control settings ref [10].

This broader background matters for semiochemical development because attractants are ultimately evaluated through movement decisions in complex sensory landscapes rather than by olfactory valence alone. An evolutionary view of insect olfaction ref [9], coupled with a cue-to-signal framework from chemical communication theory ref [11] and modern flight-tracking methodologies ref [10], therefore provides the conceptual and technical basis for designing, testing, and interpreting next-generation lures, repellents, and behaviour-modifying interventions in malaria vectors.

subsections.subsection_title: Host-Derived Olfactory Cues in Blood Feeding
subsections.content:
Host-seeking in blood-feeding mosquitoes is driven by a hierarchical interpretation of vertebrate odour blends rather than by single compounds in isolation. Comparative work on host choice shows that anthropophilic vectors such as Anopheles gambiae sensu lato and Aedes aegypti rely heavily on human-associated odour signatures, whereas more opportunistic species exhibit greater plasticity as host availability changes ref [13]. Reviews of Afrotropical malaria mosquitoes further emphasize that CO2 acts mainly as a general activator and long-range cue, while host discrimination depends on additional skin- and sweat-derived volatiles ref [4].

Among the best-supported human-linked kairomones for Anopheles are ammonia, lactic acid and carboxylic acids. In olfactometer assays, ammonia alone was attractive to An. gambiae s.s., but the strongest response emerged from synergistic blends containing ammonia, lactic acid and selected carboxylic acids, demonstrating that mixture composition is critical for host recognition ref [10]. This blend logic has been extended in An. coluzzii, where adding CO2 to a human-derived base blend substantially increased attraction and even reversed the behavioural valence of some compounds, yielding an optimized five-component lure with strong host-mimetic activity ref [7].

Electrophysiological and behavioural studies also indicate that mosquitoes detect host-associated compounds with marked context dependence. Human-specific sweat acids such as 7-octenoic acid and 3-methyl-2-hexenoic acid elicit antennal responses in An. gambiae, yet their behavioural effects can be inhibitory or modulatory depending on the accompanying odour background ref [8]. Likewise, (R)-1-octen-3-ol is not simply a universal attractant: its effect depends on release rate and blend context, altering responses differently in anthropophilic versus more generalist mosquitoes ref [12]. Together, these findings show that blood-host location is encoded by quantitative ratios and cross-component interactions, a principle central to designing semiochemical lures for surveillance and control ref [7], ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Plant and Floral Odours in Sugar Feeding
subsections.content:
Sugar feeding is a fundamental component of mosquito energy balance, and a substantial body of work shows that plant and floral odours can mediate long-range orientation to nectar sources. Early wind-tunnel studies demonstrated that both Aedes aegypti and Anopheles arabiensis orient upwind and land in response to floral odours even when visual cues are removed, establishing olfaction as a sufficient cue for nectar-source location at distance ref [8], ref [20]. These foundational results are consistent with later evidence that African malaria vectors discriminate among plant species on the basis of volatile blends rather than simply nectar presence.

In Anopheles gambiae, plant choice is not random. Field and laboratory studies indicate that males and females show preferences for particular flowering plants, and these preferences are reflected in both sugar-feeding patterns and olfactometer responses ref [9], ref [8]. Comparative analyses of common African plants found that volatiles from species such as Parthenium hysterophorus and Senna didymobotrya were especially attractive, whereas other locally abundant plants were weakly attractive or not clearly preferred ref [8]. Chemical analyses further indicate that preferred plants emit behaviorally active blends enriched in terpenoids and related compounds; in P. hysterophorus, antennally active components such as hexanal, β-pinene, limonene, β-ocimene, linalool oxide, and β-farnesene contributed to attraction, and optimized synthetic mixtures could match or exceed the attractiveness of intact plants ref [17].

More recent work has expanded this view from simple odour attraction to multimodal floral guidance. In Culex pipiens and Aedes aegypti, tansy inflorescences were most attractive when olfactory cues were combined with visual signals and floral CO2 emissions, and synthetic floral blends were further enhanced by added CO2 ref [18]. Translationally, these insights have enabled plant-based lures for malaria vectors: field-tested baits based on linalool oxide alone or in blends attracted outdoor Anopheles, including physiologically diverse individuals, supporting their utility for surveillance and potentially sugar-based control strategies ref [19]. Overall, plant odours represent a chemically diverse but operationally promising target for manipulating mosquito sugar-feeding behaviour.

Oviposition-site selection is a pivotal chemosensory decision in mosquito life history because larval stages are largely immobile and habitat quality strongly conditions offspring survival. As emphasized in broad reviews, gravid females integrate volatile attractants, contact stimulants, and deterrents from multiple sources, including microbes, conspecific immature stages and eggs, and physicochemical features of water; importantly, the same cue can be attractive or repellent depending on species and concentration ref [22], ref [23]. This complexity is especially relevant for semiochemical control, because useful lures must function beyond close-range stimulation and under field conditions.

Evidence for specific oviposition semiochemicals now spans several mosquito genera. In Culex quinquefasciatus, egg-raft apical droplets contain the pheromone erythro-6-acetoxy-5-hexadecanolide, which attracts gravid females and promotes aggregation around previously used sites ref [25]. More recently, a reverse chemical ecology strategy identified acetaldehyde as an oviposition attractant for the same species, linking receptor-based screening to behavioral activity ref [10]. In malaria vectors, cedrol was identified from attractive soil infusions and shown to increase oviposition in laboratory assays, attract gravid Anopheles gambiae s.l. in semi-field systems, and enhance trap catches in the field, providing rare support for a long-range oviposition attractant in anophelines ref [26].

Microbial and conspecific cues are particularly prominent in container breeders. In Aedes aegypti, bacteria associated with bamboo and oak infusions mediate oviposition preferences, and bioassay-guided analyses implicated bacteria-derived carboxylic acids and methyl esters as key stimulatory signals ref [27]. Egg-derived cues also contribute: extracts from conspecific eggs contain fatty acids and related compounds that can elicit positive or negative oviposition responses depending on molecule and dose ref [8]. Together, these studies suggest that oviposition cues often encode habitat suitability indirectly—through signals of microbial productivity, prior conspecific use, or both—making them attractive candidates for gravid traps and attract-and-kill strategies ref [22], ref [23].

subsections.subsection_title: Pheromones and Other Chemical Signals Linked to Feeding-Related Life History
subsections.content:
Although pheromone research in mosquitoes has often focused on oviposition, a smaller but conceptually important literature links semiochemicals to mating and, indirectly, to feeding-related life history. Because successful mating determines the production of blood-feeding and ovipositing females, aggregation and sex-recognition signals are relevant to population dynamics even when they do not directly guide a feeding act. Early studies in Culiseta inornata concluded that volatile female-derived cues could stimulate male sexual responses independently of flight sound, indicating that chemical signals can participate in mate location in at least some culicids ref [6]. Likewise, work on Stegomyia mosquitoes provided evidence for a contact sexual pheromone used after close-range encounter, with male tarsi implicated in species recognition and reproductive isolation ref [7].

In Aedes aegypti, lek-like swarm formation has been repeatedly linked to aggregation pheromones. Laboratory and semi-field experiments showed that swarming males, and possibly females, emit olfactory cues that increase flight activity and aggregation, thereby modulating mating opportunities ref [32]. Subsequent chemical analyses identified candidate swarm-associated volatiles, including ketoisophorone-related compounds and 1-(4-ethylphenyl)ethanone, and showed that at least some of these compounds altered female attraction or male swarm-like activity under laboratory conditions ref [28]. These findings support a model in which acoustic signals initiate close-range sexual interactions, while chemical cues help structure swarm assembly and persistence ref [28], ref [32].

From a control perspective, these signals matter because mating success constrains the efficacy of sterile-male, incompatible-male, and gene-drive programmes. Reviews of male mosquito mating behaviour have therefore argued that better characterization of swarm cues—including visual, acoustic, and possible chemical components—could improve male release quality, enable swarm-targeted lure-and-kill tactics, and refine monitoring tools ref [8]. However, compared with host odours or oviposition attractants, mosquito mating pheromones remain less chemically resolved and less consistently validated in the field. Thus, they represent a promising but still underdeveloped frontier for semiochemical-based mosquito control ref [8], ref [28], ref [6].

Cuticular and chemotaxonomic signatures occupy a distinctive position within mosquito chemical ecology because they are largely non-volatile, surface-associated cues that can encode species, sex and physiological state. Early work on the Anopheles gambiae complex showed that adults of An. gambiae and An. arabiensis could be differentiated by gas-chromatographic analysis of cuticular hydrocarbons, despite their morphological similarity, with species-level differences particularly evident in the relative abundance of female n-paraffins around C26–C29 ref [33]. This approach was extended to individual mosquitoes, where ratios among selected paraffinic and methyl-branched peaks provided statistically significant markers for both females and, to a lesser extent, males ref [34].

These studies are important not only for taxonomy but also for semiochemical interpretation. In Aedes aegypti, detailed GC and GC-MS profiling identified a chemically diverse epicuticular blend comprising n-alkanes, monomethylalkanes, dimethylalkanes and at least one alkene, with quantitative variation across sex, age and strain ref [35]. Females carried significantly higher amounts of several higher-molecular-weight branched hydrocarbons than males, and age-dependent shifts were also pronounced, indicating that cuticular profiles are dynamic rather than fixed labels ref [35]. Comparable use of hydrocarbon patterns to separate sibling or closely related mosquitoes has also been demonstrated in Anopheles culicifacies and the Anopheles maculipennis complex, supporting the broader value of chemotaxonomic markers across Culicidae.

For control-oriented semiochemical research, the main significance of these signatures is twofold. First, they can improve species and population discrimination where vector complexes differ in host use, feeding ecology or intervention susceptibility. Second, because cuticular hydrocarbons in other dipterans function in close-range recognition and mating, mosquito surface lipids remain plausible candidates for contact-mediated signalling linked indirectly to feeding-related life history, even when direct behavioural evidence is still limited ref [34], ref [35]. Thus, cuticular chemistry forms a useful bridge between chemical taxonomy and functional semiochemistry.

subsections.subsection_title: Translational Applications for Oviposition Monitoring and Control
subsections.content:
Translation of oviposition semiochemistry into operational tools has focused on gravid-female surveillance and, increasingly, on attract-and-kill concepts. A notable example is the chemically baited ovitrap developed for Aedes aegypti, in which a four-component blend of n-heneicosane, skatole, p-cresol, and phenol increased egg deposition relative to a standard ovitrap under laboratory conditions, with the optimized trap retaining activity for about three days ref [36]. This study illustrates both the promise and the practical constraints of semiochemical deployment: efficacy depends not only on blend composition, but also on trap architecture, dispenser format, and lure longevity ref [36].

Field surveillance studies likewise show that chemical baiting can substantially improve trap performance, although most operational systems for container-breeding Aedes have so far emphasized host-seeking rather than gravid responses. In suburban Florida, counterflow traps baited with CO2 and kairomonal lures outperformed conventional CDC and Aedes-specific traps for Aedes albopictus collection, underscoring how odor release, visual design, and airflow geometry jointly determine capture efficiency ref [8]. In Kenya, adding a human-odor-derived component, especially hexanoic acid with CO2, to BG-Sentinel traps approximately doubled Aedes aegypti captures relative to the commercial lure, while some multicomponent blends reduced performance, highlighting the risk of antagonistic interactions in lure design ref [9].

For oviposition-based control, these findings imply that successful translational products will likely require species-specific optimization rather than simple accumulation of attractive compounds. Earlier surveillance work with infusion-enhanced ovitraps and sticky ovitraps already demonstrated that oviposition cues can be harnessed for sensitive detection and adult suppression, but also revealed problems of instability and context dependence in natural baits. Synthetic blends offer greater standardization and manufacturability than fermenting infusions, yet their short field life and variable synergy remain key bottlenecks ref [36]. Future systems will therefore need to integrate semiochemistry with improved dispensers, trap engineering, and local validation to convert laboratory oviposition cues into robust monitoring and control technologies.

General reviews of mosquito oviposition semiochemistry consistently emphasize that gravid females integrate chemical, visual, tactile, and physiological information across sequential stages of habitat assessment, from long-range orientation to short-range acceptance and egg deposition. A central contribution of the classical synthesis by Bentley and Day was to formalize this process behaviorally and terminologically, distinguishing attractants and repellents from stimulants and deterrents while stressing that many published assays conflate these categories because they do not isolate olfactory from contact effects ref [21].

Subsequent reviews expanded this framework by organizing oviposition cues according to ecological source. Navarro-Silva et al. highlighted the breadth of semiochemical classes implicated in site choice, including pheromones from eggs and other immature stages, kairomonal signals from plant infusions and microbes, and deterrent compounds associated with unsuitable habitats, while also arguing that these cues could support more sustainable surveillance and control if translated carefully into traps and lures ref [39]. Afify and Galizia further systematized the literature across mosquito taxa, showing that responses are highly context dependent, varying with species, cue concentration, prior larval experience, and assay design, which helps explain apparently contradictory reports for the same compound ref [22].

Taken together, these reviews establish several recurring themes for the field: oviposition signalling is multimodal rather than purely olfactory; microbial and detrital habitat chemistry often provides dominant information about larval resource quality; conspecific-derived cues can either promote aggregation or signal overcrowding; and ecological relevance must be validated beyond laboratory choice assays ref [21], ref [39], ref [22]. They also converge on a translational caution particularly relevant to control: semiochemicals rarely act as universal lures, so species-specific calibration, dose optimization, and field validation are prerequisites before deployment in monitoring or attract-and-kill systems ref [39], ref [22].

Microbial metabolism and broader aquatic habitat chemistry are central components of mosquito oviposition-site assessment. In container-breeding Aedes, fermenting plant infusions consistently outperform clean water, and elegant filtration and replacement experiments have shown that the oviposition-stimulating activity resides largely with microorganisms rather than the infusion water per se ref [40]. In Ae. aegypti, bacterial communities isolated from bamboo and oak leaf infusions elicited strong egg-laying responses, and bioassay-guided fractionation linked this activity to bacteria-associated carboxylic acids and methyl esters, including nonanoic acid, tetradecanoic acid and methyl tetradecanoate ref [40]. Earlier work on Aedes albopictus likewise implicated bacteria in oak-leaf infusion-mediated oviposition, reinforcing the view that microbes help define habitat quality across container systems.

For African malaria vectors, the relevant signals appear to emerge from interactions among habitat age, physicochemical state, microbes and emitted volatiles rather than from any single cue alone. Field experiments with wild Anopheles arabiensis showed that freshly prepared ponds received about twice as many early-instar larvae as ponds aged 4 or 17 days before access, indicating active preference for less persistent habitats ref [3]. These fresher ponds were associated with higher turbidity, higher temperature, elevated nitrite, and lower pH and chlorophyll, and they also differed in bacterial profiles on a round-dependent basis ref [3]. Notably, 4-heptanone, 2-ethylhexanal and an octenal isomer were detected only from fresh ponds, highlighting how microbial succession and water chemistry can translate into volatile signatures relevant to gravid females ref [3].

Mechanistically, these studies support a layered model in which mosquitoes use long-range volatile cues to locate candidate water bodies and short-range/contact cues linked to microbial cells or metabolites to accept or reject them. This framework is consistent with demonstrations that Anopheles gambiae responds to volatiles from bacteria-containing media ref [4], although not all bacterial effects are attractive and responses may depend on community composition, density and environmental context ref [3], ref [5], ref [6]. The practical implication is that microbial and aquatic habitat signals are promising but inherently dynamic targets for lure design, because attractive blends likely represent particular stages of habitat succession rather than static compounds alone ref [40], ref [3], ref [7].

Conspecific cues can function as true pheromones, but their effects are often species-specific, concentration-dependent, and embedded within broader habitat assessment. The strongest classical example comes from Culex quinquefasciatus, in which apical droplets on freshly laid egg rafts attract gravid females and thereby promote aggregation at previously used sites ref [23]. Chemical characterization identified the major volatile component as erythro-6-acetoxy-5-hexadecanolide, and synthetic material reproduced the oviposition-attractant activity observed with natural egg-raft extracts ref [41], ref [23].

Follow-up behavioral work established that this Culex signal is highly structure-dependent: activity was lost when the lactone was opened, the carbon chain shortened, or the stereochemistry altered, with evidence that the natural active form is the (-)-(5R,6S) enantiomer ref [23]. Importantly, the compound appears to be produced by the mosquito rather than by associated microbes, being present in mature ovaries before oviposition and remaining associated with egg rafts after deposition ref [23]. These findings support its status as a bona fide oviposition pheromone rather than a purely microbial by-product.

By contrast, conspecific egg-derived signalling in Aedes aegypti appears more chemically heterogeneous and less easily reduced to a single pheromone. Egg extracts contain multiple lactones, fatty acids, and methyl esters, with some acids such as dodecanoic acid and (Z)-9-hexadecenoic acid promoting oviposition, whereas several methyl esters act as deterrents, suggesting a blend-based system that may balance attraction with avoidance of overcrowding ref [26]. More recently, receptor-guided screening in Cx. quinquefasciatus identified acetaldehyde as an oviposition attractant for gravid females, illustrating how reverse chemical ecology can uncover additional conspecific-associated or oviposition-relevant cues beyond the historically defined egg pheromone ref [27]. Collectively, these studies indicate that mosquitoes exploit both dedicated pheromonal signals and broader conspecific-derived chemical signatures when selecting oviposition sites.

subsections.subsection_title: Plant- and Fungi-Derived Volatiles in Oviposition Site Choice
subsections.content:
Plant-derived volatiles can shape oviposition decisions by signalling both the presence of suitable aquatic habitat and the likely nutritional context for larvae. In African malaria vectors, this link is especially evident for grasses and crop plants associated with productive breeding sites. Gravid Anopheles arabiensis and An. coluzzii respond hierarchically to volatile extracts from emergent grasses, with Poaceae-associated cues generally eliciting stronger attraction and oviposition than cues from Typha or papyrus, consistent with larval distributions in the field ref [44].

Cultivated grasses extend this logic into agroecosystems. Rice odours attract gravid An. arabiensis across plant phenological stages, stimulate oviposition, and can be reduced to an electrophysiologically active synthetic blend that remains attractive under semi-field conditions ref [45]. Similarly, sugarcane pollen-associated volatiles attract and stimulate oviposition in gravid An. arabiensis, and comparative assays suggest overlap with other grass-derived cue spaces, including shared components such as alpha-pinene and nonanal ref [5]. Together with evidence that maize pollen odours also attract gravid An. arabiensis, these studies support the idea that grasses provide a chemically coherent class of habitat-associated signals that can be exploited for gravid-targeted surveillance and control.

Fungi can also contribute to ostensibly plant-linked oviposition signals. Cedrol, the first confirmed oviposition attractant for members of the Anopheles gambiae complex, was traced to Fusarium spp. isolated from rhizomes of Cyperus rotundus collected at a natural breeding site, showing that some 'plant-associated' cues may in fact be microbially generated within plant–soil interfaces ref [43]. This complicates simple source attribution, but it also broadens the translational opportunity: effective lures may emerge from plant, pollen, or fungal metabolism, provided they reliably indicate habitats preferred by gravid females ref [43], ref [44], ref [45], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Attractive Toxic Sugar Baits and Lure-and-Kill Strategies
subsections.content:
Attractive toxic sugar baits (ATSBs) and related lure-and-kill devices exploit two robust elements of mosquito chemical ecology: the need for plant-derived sugar meals and the orientation of host-seeking females to attractive odour plumes. ATSBs are particularly appealing as supplementary tools for residual transmission because they can target both sexes and can act outside houses, where long-lasting insecticidal nets and indoor residual spraying are less effective [1]. Early field studies showed that vegetation-applied or station-based ATSBs could markedly suppress anopheline populations, establishing proof-of-concept for semiochemical-guided killing at landscape scale [3][4].

Recent optimization work has refined this concept for African malaria vectors. An ivermectin-based ATSB developed for Anopheles arabiensis caused >95% mortality within 48 h at 0.01% ivermectin, and importantly showed that bait architecture and placement strongly influenced uptake: resting-site-like prototypes outperformed simpler feeding surfaces, and deployment near peri-domestic vegetation increased feeding relative to positions nearer huts [1]. These findings reinforce that attractancy is not determined by sugar chemistry alone, but by the integration of olfactory, visual, and microhabitat cues associated with natural sugar foraging [5][6].

Lure-and-kill strategies based on host odours extend the same principle to blood-seeking females. The Mosquito Landing Box, baited with human odours, attracted significantly more An. arabiensis and An. funestus than unbaited controls, and its peak visitation coincided with periods of human outdoor activity, highlighting its relevance for outdoor exposure [2]. However, vectors often contacted the device only briefly, so mortality with surface-applied pirimiphos-methyl remained moderate, indicating that successful outdoor kill stations require toxicants effective after very short contact, or alternative agents such as fungi or electrocuting surfaces [2][7][8]. Overall, ATSBs and odour-baited killing devices illustrate how semiochemicals can be coupled to toxic delivery, but also how field efficacy depends critically on formulation, device design, placement, and the behavioural context of target species.

subsections.subsection_title: Odour-Baited Traps for Surveillance and Field Evaluation
subsections.content:
Odour-baited traps are central to translating semiochemical discoveries into operational surveillance tools because they provide a standardized way to compare lure blends, trap designs, and deployment contexts under field conditions. For malaria vectors, progress has relied on combining carbon dioxide with host-derived kairomones that mimic human odour, thereby improving sensitivity relative to unbaited or visually based devices. Foundational work on Afrotropical malaria mosquitoes established the behavioural relevance of odour cues for long-range orientation, while later studies showed that blends containing ammonia, lactic acid, carboxylic acids, and related human volatiles can act synergistically rather than independently in trap-based assays [ref 2, ref 3, ref 4].

Field evaluation has increasingly focused on simple, scalable devices suitable for routine surveillance in endemic settings. In Ethiopia, an odour-baited sticky trap paired with efficient attractant blends was shown to detect Anopheles arabiensis effectively, illustrating the value of low-cost formats for monitoring outdoor and peri-domestic vector activity [ref 1]. Related studies in East Africa reported improved odour baits for Aedes aegypti surveillance and demonstrated that chemically based trap optimization can substantially increase capture efficiency, species selectivity, and consistency across ecological settings [ref 5, ref 6]. Comparative trap studies further emphasize that lure performance is inseparable from trap architecture, airflow, release rate, and local vector community composition [ref 7].

From a semiochemical perspective, these evaluations do more than identify practical surveillance tools: they provide iterative feedback for refining synthetic attractants. Trap catches can reveal whether a candidate blend is broadly attractive, species-biased, or context dependent, and they help bridge laboratory electrophysiology and behavioural assays with epidemiologically relevant field performance. Accordingly, odour-baited surveillance remains a critical intermediate step between volatile identification and deployment of lure-and-kill or mass-trapping interventions [ref 2, ref 4, ref 8].

subsections.subsection_title: Human-Derived Volatiles as a Basis for Synthetic Attractants
subsections.content:
Human-derived volatiles provide the most direct chemical starting point for synthetic host odours because mosquitoes orient to a blend of cues emitted from breath, skin and associated microbiota rather than to any single universal compound. A broad survey of the healthy human volatolome documented more than 1800 volatile organic compounds across breath, skin secretions, saliva, blood, urine and faeces, underscoring both the richness of candidate ligands and the need to identify the behaviorally relevant subset for mosquito attraction ref [49]. This complexity helps explain why attractive formulations based on human odour typically rely on simplified blends that capture dominant and repeatable kairomonal features rather than attempting to reproduce the entire human scent bouquet.

Work on malaria vectors established that common human emanations such as ammonia, lactic acid and selected carboxylic acids act synergistically in host seeking, providing an early proof that blend composition matters more than single-compound activity ref [2]. Subsequent electrophysiological and behavioural studies showed that Anopheles gambiae detects human-specific sweat constituents, while context-dependent responses to generic host volatiles such as (R)-1-octen-3-ol further emphasized that mosquito attraction depends on the presence of a complementary odour background ref [3], ref [4]. Importantly, carbon dioxide is not merely an added attractant but a key gating cue that strongly enhances orientation to human-derived blends and remains central to synthetic lure design ref [5].

These insights have translated into operational attractants for surveillance and control. Odour-bait studies in Afrotropical malaria mosquitoes demonstrated that synthetic host blends can reproduce substantial components of human attractiveness in the field ref [6]. More recently, improved monitoring lures for Aedes aegypti and related vectors have combined human-derived volatiles with optimized release systems to increase trap sensitivity under realistic deployment conditions ref [7]. Overall, the trajectory from cataloguing human VOCs to identifying synergistic subsets illustrates a central principle in semiochemical control: effective synthetic attractants are best viewed as parsimonious reconstructions of human odour space, tuned to mosquito sensory ecology rather than exhaustive chemical mimicry ref [49], ref [5].
